cls: Immunomodulatory cytokine / disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis (type I interferon)
pharm: A glycosylated recombinant human interferon beta produced in Chinese hamster ovary cells with the same amino acid sequence as natural interferon beta; it binds type I interferon receptors to exert immunomodulatory, antiviral, and antiproliferative effects that reduce relapse frequency and MRI lesion activity in relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis.
quick: Avonex 30 mcg IM once weekly; Rebif 44 mcg SC three times weekly
Not relevant (injectable); take antipyretic to ease flu-like symptoms
Use only if benefit justifies risk; data do not show major malformation increase
Minimal milk transfer; considered compatible with breastfeeding
Caution; hepatotoxicity reported - monitor LFTs, reduce/stop if elevated
Avoid heavy use; adds to hepatic risk
summary: Interferon beta-1a is a recombinant type I interferon used as a disease-modifying therapy for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (including clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease). Two FDA-approved products differ in route and frequency: Avonex is 30 mcg intramuscularly once weekly, and Rebif is 44 mcg (or 22 mcg) subcutaneously three times weekly. It reduces relapse rate, slows accumulation of disability, and decreases MRI lesion burden. Key safety concerns are hepatotoxicity (including rare hepatic failure), depression and suicidal ideation, flu-like symptoms, injection-site reactions (especially with subcutaneous Rebif), bone marrow suppression (leukopenia), and thyroid dysfunction. Neutralizing antibodies can develop and may reduce efficacy. It is not a cure and does not reverse fixed disability.
indications: Relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, including clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease
Avonex: also used to delay progression to clinically definite MS in patients with a first clinical demyelinating event (CIS) with MRI features consistent with MS

dosage.n: Titration not required but starting at 7.5 mcg and increasing by 7.5 mcg weekly over 4 weeks to 30 mcg may reduce flu-like symptoms

dosage.d: 44 mcg (or 22 mcg in patients who cannot tolerate the higher dose)
dosage.n: Titrate over 4 weeks: weeks 1-2 give 20% of dose, weeks 3-4 give 50%, then full dose; give doses on the same 3 days each week (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri), at least 48 h apart, preferably late afternoon/evening

dosage.d: Acetaminophen or NSAID before and for up to 24 h after each injection
dosage.n: Dosing at bedtime can lessen perceived symptoms

dosage.d: Reduce dose or interrupt therapy until laboratory values recover
dosage.n: Permanently discontinue for hepatic failure or severe persistent abnormalities

admin: Avonex is given intramuscularly once weekly; Rebif is given subcutaneously three times weekly - do not interchange dosing without prescriber guidance
Allow refrigerated product to reach room temperature before injecting to reduce discomfort
Rotate injection sites with each subcutaneous dose to minimize site reactions and necrosis
Premedicate with acetaminophen or an NSAID to reduce flu-like symptoms; consider dose titration at initiation
Train patients (or caregivers) in aseptic self-injection technique; use the autoinjector or prefilled syringe as supplied
Do not use if the solution is discolored or contains particulate matter
moa: Interferon beta-1a binds to type I interferon receptors (IFNAR) on the cell surface, triggering JAK-STAT signaling and transcription of interferon-stimulated genes. In multiple sclerosis its benefit is attributed to immunomodulation: it shifts the cytokine balance away from pro-inflammatory Th1 responses toward anti-inflammatory profiles, reduces antigen presentation and T-cell proliferation, decreases pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and reduces the migration of activated leukocytes across the blood-brain barrier by downregulating adhesion molecules and matrix metalloproteinases. The net effect is reduced inflammatory demyelinating activity, fewer relapses, and decreased MRI gadolinium-enhancing and T2 lesions. The exact mechanism by which it exerts its effects in MS is not fully understood.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to natural or recombinant interferon beta, human albumin, or any product component
relative: History of depression, suicidal ideation, or other significant psychiatric disorder
Pre-existing significant hepatic disease or elevated transaminases
Severe cardiac disease (flu-like symptoms may worsen cardiac status)
monitor: Liver function tests (hepatotoxicity, rare hepatic failure)
Complete blood count with differential (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia)
Signs of thrombotic microangiopathy and new/worsening seizures

preg: Available data from postmarketing registries and cohort studies have not established a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage; some earlier reports suggested possible low birth weight or spontaneous abortion at high doses in animals. Interferon beta-1a should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk. Many clinicians continue therapy in women at high relapse risk after individualized counseling.
lact: Interferon beta-1a is a large glycoprotein that is excreted into breast milk in only minimal amounts and is expected to be degraded in the infant gastrointestinal tract, so systemic absorption by the infant is negligible. It is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is recommended for renal impairment. Interferon beta is catabolized like other proteins and is not predominantly renally cleared; however, exercise general caution and monitor as clinically indicated.
hepatic: Hepatic injury, including asymptomatic transaminase elevation, hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and rare cases of severe hepatic failure (some fatal or requiring transplant), has been reported. Use caution in patients with pre-existing liver disease, active alcohol use, or concomitant hepatotoxic drugs. Monitor liver function tests at baseline and periodically; reduce dose or discontinue if transaminases rise markedly or signs of hepatic dysfunction (jaundice, coagulopathy) appear.

major: Other hepatotoxic agents - additive risk of liver injury
Myelosuppressive agents - additive bone marrow suppression
moderate: Drugs that are sensitive CYP substrates - interferons can modulate hepatic CYP450 enzymes, potentially altering levels of co-administered drugs
Live vaccines - immune response may be altered
minor: No significant interaction reported with most disease-modifying MS therapies, but combinations should be individualized
interactions.food: Not applicable for an injectable; no food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid heavy alcohol use, which adds to hepatotoxicity risk and may worsen depression.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause transaminase, blood count, and thyroid function abnormalities; neutralizing antibodies may interfere with assays and reduce biologic activity. Interferon may alter results of laboratory tests measuring liver and blood parameters.

serious: Hepatotoxicity including hepatitis and rare hepatic failure
New or worsening cardiac disease / cardiomyopathy
emergency: Thrombotic microangiopathy (new thrombocytopenia with hemolysis and renal failure)

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline, then at 1, 3, and 6 months and periodically thereafter
Complete blood count with differential and platelets at baseline and periodically
Thyroid function tests periodically, especially with prior thyroid disease
Mood and screening for depression and suicidal ideation at each visit
Clinical relapse rate and MRI activity to assess efficacy
Consider neutralizing antibody testing if loss of efficacy
counsel: Flu-like symptoms (fever, aches, chills) are common at first and usually fade over weeks; taking acetaminophen or ibuprofen before your shot and injecting at bedtime helps
Rotate where you inject each time and let the medicine warm to room temperature to reduce skin reactions
Tell your doctor right away if you feel depressed, hopeless, or have thoughts of harming yourself
Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, easy bruising or bleeding, or unusual sleepiness - these can signal liver or blood problems
Keep all blood-test appointments so your liver, blood counts, and thyroid can be checked
Avoid heavy alcohol use and tell your doctor about all other medicines you take
This medicine reduces flare-ups but does not cure MS; keep using it even when you feel well unless your doctor says to stop
Store in the refrigerator and do not freeze; protect from light
pk: Biologic (interferon-response) markers rise within hours; clinical benefit over weeks to months
IM (Avonex) serum Tmax ~3-15 h; SC (Rebif) Tmax ~16 h
Serum elimination half-life ~10 h (Avonex) and ~50-69 h (Rebif), though biologic effect outlasts serum levels
Pharmacodynamic effects persist over the dosing interval (weekly IM or three-times-weekly SC)
Refrigerate 2-8 C; do not freeze; protect from light; may keep at room temperature for limited time per labeling
pearls: Two FDA-approved formulations: Avonex 30 mcg IM once weekly vs Rebif 44 mcg SC three times weekly - confirm which product before dosing
Hepatotoxicity (including rare hepatic failure) and depression/suicidality are the key boxed safety concerns - monitor LFTs and mood proactively
Premedicate with acetaminophen/NSAID and titrate the dose to blunt flu-like symptoms, which improve over the first weeks
Check CBC and thyroid function periodically; leukopenia and thyroid dysfunction are common
Neutralizing antibodies (NABs) can develop and reduce efficacy - consider testing when relapses recur despite adherence
Injection-site necrosis is a subcutaneous (Rebif) concern - reinforce site rotation and inspection
Not a cure: it lowers relapse rate and MRI activity but does not reverse established disability
missed: For weekly Avonex, take the missed dose as soon as you remember, then continue on your usual day, keeping doses at least a few days apart. For three-times-weekly Rebif, take the missed dose as soon as you remember and resume your normal schedule, but do not give two doses on the same day or within 48 hours of each other. Do not double up to make up a missed dose; contact your healthcare provider if you are unsure.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Excessive dosing may intensify flu-like symptoms, bone marrow suppression, and transaminase elevations. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring of hepatic and hematologic parameters and symptomatic treatment.
